meta.blurb: A student in Los Angeles tries to log in to a computer 560 kilometres away, and it crashes after two letters. That evening in 1969 is one of eleven dated days, from Columbus to Gagarin, that each opened a door to change.
meta.bible: Eleven Days: a short history of eleven dated days, told in order; the voice is clear, fair and curious, honest about suffering and debate, with no invented numbers, dates or quotes; no real living people are named. Introduction: 1752 in Britain, when Wednesday 2 September was followed by Thursday 14 September because the Julian calendar had drifted eleven days; Pope Gregory XIII had reformed it in 1582 for Catholic Europe. Julian, Gregorian. Day 1, 12 October 1492: Christopher Columbus, a Genoese sailor in Spanish service, left Palos on 3 August 1492 with the Santa Maria, the Pinta and the Nina and landed in the Bahamas on an island the Taino people called Guanahani (which island is debated); he thought he had reached Asia; West Indies. Taino. Columbian Exchange: potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies, cocoa one way; wheat, sugar cane, horses, cattle the other; smallpox and measles devastated the Americas; enslaved Africans were later carried across the Atlantic. Day 2, 14 May 1796: Edward Jenner, country doctor in Gloucestershire, used cowpox from the milkmaid Sarah Nelmes on James Phipps, aged eight, son of his gardener; vaccine from the Latin vacca, cow; the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated on 8 May 1980. Smallpox, Cowpox, Inoculation, Vaccine, Milkmaid, Milkmaids. Day 3, 4 September 1882: Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station in lower Manhattan, New York; Joseph Swan in England also made bulbs; steam engines burning coal. Edison, Swan, Menlo Park, New Jersey, Manhattan, Generators, Filament. Day 4, 17 December 1903: Wilbur and Orville Wright of Dayton, Ohio, bicycle makers; Kitty Hawk, North Carolina; the Flyer; first flight twelve seconds and about thirty-seven metres, the last of four flights fifty-nine seconds and about two hundred and sixty metres; John Alcock and Arthur Whitten Brown crossed the Atlantic non-stop in 1919. Day 5, 28 June 1914: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, and his wife Sophie were shot in Sarajevo, Bosnia, by Gavrilo Princip, aged nineteen, a Bosnian Serb nationalist; war began within about five weeks; the armistice was on 11 November 1918; about nine million soldiers died; four empires fell (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, Ottoman). Serbia, Belgium, Armistice. Day 6, 16 July 1945: the Trinity test at 5:29 in the morning in the New Mexico desert; Manhattan Project; Los Alamos laboratory directed by Robert Oppenheimer; Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found fission in 1938, explained by Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch; Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945; no nuclear weapon used in war since. Fission, Nucleus, Uranium, Nazi, Einstein, Bhagavad Gita, Hindu. Day 7, 15 August 1947: India's independence; Britain ruled much of India for nearly two centuries, directly after 1858; Mahatma Gandhi and the Salt March of 1930; Jawaharlal Nehru's speech of the tryst with destiny; Cyril Radcliffe drew the borders in about five weeks; perhaps fifteen million migrated; deaths estimated from several hundred thousand to about two million; Gandhi spent the day in Calcutta fasting and praying for peace. Partition, Pakistan, Hindu, Muslim, Congress, Crown, East India Company. Day 8, 10 December 1948: Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in Paris at the Palais de Chaillot, 48 in favour, none against, eight abstentions, two absent; thirty articles; drafting committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt with Peng Chun Chang, Charles Malik, Rene Cassin and Hansa Mehta; United Nations. Human Rights Day. Day 9, 25 April 1953: Nature published the double helix paper of Francis Crick and a young American colleague (not named); Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 at King's College London; Maurice Wilkins; Franklin died in 1958 aged thirty-seven; the Nobel Prize of 1962; Human Genome Project 2003; DNA. Day 10, 12 April 1961: Yuri Gagarin, aged twenty-seven, Vostok 1, from Baikonur, one orbit, one hundred and eight minutes; Sputnik on 4 October 1957; Neil Armstrong on the Moon on 20 July 1969 from the lunar module Eagle; Soviet Union, Cold War, Kazakhstan, Volga. Day 11, 29 October 1969: first message on the ARPANET, from a student at the University of California in Los Angeles to the Stanford Research Institute about 560 kilometres away; the letters LO before the crash; Ray Tomlinson's email in 1971; shared rules in 1983; World Wide Web about 1990 at CERN (inventor not named); more than five billion internet users. Internet, Packet. Magna Carta 1215, Berlin Wall 1989. Britain, British, America, American, Americas, Europe, European, Asia, Africa, Atlantic, Russia, Russian, Japan, Japanese, Hiroshima, Nagasaki, Canada, Spain, Spanish, Italian, English, Latin.

A1A2: In 1752, Britain lost eleven days from its calendar.
This book visits eleven other days that changed the world.
We will visit them in order, from the oldest to the newest.
In 1492, Columbus sailed west from Spain with three ships.
On 12 October 1492, the sailors reached an island with people living on it.
Potatoes, corn and tomatoes crossed the ocean to Europe.
New diseases also came, and many people died of them.
Smallpox was a terrible disease that killed many people.
Edward Jenner was a country doctor in England.
On 14 May 1796, Jenner tested his idea on a young boy.
In 1980, the world announced that smallpox was gone for ever.
Before electric light, people used candles and lamps at night.
Thomas Edison and others made a glass bulb that gave light.
On 4 September 1882, a power station in New York started working.
Soon cities everywhere built power stations and put up wires.
The Wright brothers made bicycles and dreamed of flying.
On 17 December 1903, Orville Wright flew for twelve seconds.
Planes improved quickly, and soon they could cross the ocean.
A trip that took weeks by ship now takes only hours.
In 1914, Europe's big countries had large armies and many promises.
A young man shot the Archduke and his wife in Sarajevo.
Within weeks, many countries were at war with each other.
The war lasted more than four years, and millions died.
In 1938, scientists found a way to split the atom.
A huge secret project began in the United States.
On 16 July 1945, the first atomic bomb exploded in a desert.
Nuclear weapons have not been used in war since 1945.
For many years, Britain ruled India, and many Indians wanted freedom.
In 1947, Britain agreed to leave, and India was divided.
At midnight, India became a free country, and crowds celebrated.
Millions of people crossed the new borders, and many suffered.
After the war, nations wanted to protect the rights of everyone.
On 10 December 1948, the nations voted to accept the Declaration.
It says that all people are born free and equal.
It is not a law, but it has changed many laws.
Scientists believed that DNA held the plans for life.
Scientists in London and Cambridge worked hard to find its shape.
DNA looks like a twisted ladder with two long strands.
Today, doctors and scientists read DNA to fight disease.
In 1957, the Soviet Union sent a small satellite into space.
On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space.
Gagarin returned safely to Earth and landed in a field.
In 1969, people walked on the Moon for the first time.
In the 1960s, computers were huge, rare and could not talk to each other.
On 29 October 1969, one computer sent a message to another.
More computers joined the network, and people began to send email.
Today, billions of people use the internet every day.
Each day came after a long time of work and ideas.
Not every change was good for everyone, and many days are missing.
The next day that changes the world may be today.
B1B2: In September 1752, people in Britain went to bed on the second and woke up on the fourteenth. The old calendar had drifted away from the seasons, so eleven days were removed to set it right.
This book is about eleven other days, each of which opened a door to a changed world. Big changes rarely happen in a single day, but one day can show the moment when a change became visible.
Each day has a date that we know, and a story of what came before and what followed. We will visit them in order, from 1492 to 1969, and you may well think of other days that deserve a place.
On 3 August 1492, an Italian sailor named Christopher Columbus left Spain with three small ships. He was working for the king and queen of Spain, and he hoped to reach Asia by sailing west.

After more than a month at sea, the ships reached an island in the Bahamas early on 12 October 1492. The island was already home to the Taíno people, who called it Guanahani, but Columbus believed he had reached the edge of Asia.

Over the following centuries, foods such as potatoes, maize, tomatoes and chocolate crossed the Atlantic from the Americas to the rest of the world. Wheat, sugar cane, horses and cattle travelled the other way, and the world's diets changed for ever.

The exchange also carried diseases such as smallpox and measles, which had never before been known in the Americas. People there had no protection, and historians believe that millions died, although the numbers are debated.
In the 1700s, smallpox killed hundreds of thousands of people in Europe every year. Those who survived were often left with deep scars, and some were blinded.

Edward Jenner worked as a country doctor in Gloucestershire, in the west of England. Local people told him that milkmaids who had caught the mild illness called cowpox from cows seldom caught smallpox.
On 14 May 1796, Jenner took a little fluid from a milkmaid's cowpox sore. He rubbed it into small cuts on the arm of an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps, who soon recovered from a mild illness.

The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for a cow, and the idea soon spread around the world. After a huge global effort, the World Health Organization declared in 1980 that smallpox had been wiped out, the first human disease ever to disappear.
Before the arrival of electric light, evenings were lit by candles, oil lamps and gas flames. They gave a weak light, they often smelled, and they could easily start a fire.

Around 1879, Edison and his team in New Jersey made a practical light bulb, and Joseph Swan did similar work in England. Lighting one room was not enough, because the real challenge was to supply a whole city with power.

On 4 September 1882, Edison's Pearl Street power station in New York City began to send electricity to nearby buildings. Steam engines burning coal turned the generators, and the first customers included a newspaper office.
Power stations and wires soon spread across the world, bringing light, motors, trams and later fridges and radios. Even today, hundreds of millions of people still have no reliable electricity.

Wilbur and Orville Wright repaired and built bicycles in Dayton, Ohio, but they dreamed of building a flying machine. They studied birds, built gliders and made a small wind tunnel, because the hardest problem was control.

On the windy sands of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903, Orville Wright flew their machine for twelve seconds. It covered about 37 metres, which is shorter than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet.

Aeroplanes improved at astonishing speed, and in 1919 two British airmen, Alcock and Brown, flew non-stop across the Atlantic. Within sixty-six years of Kitty Hawk, human beings had walked on the Moon.

Today a journey that once took weeks by ship takes just a few hours by air. In 2019, airlines carried more than four billion passengers, although flying also adds to the pollution that warms the planet.

In 1914, the great powers of Europe had huge armies and a web of promises to defend one another. On 28 June, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, visited the city of Sarajevo with his wife Sophie.

Earlier that morning, someone had thrown a bomb at the royal car, but it missed its target. Later, the driver took a wrong turn, and Gavrilo Princip, a nineteen-year-old nationalist, shot and killed the Archduke and his wife.

Austria-Hungary blamed neighbouring Serbia for the murders, and a chain of alliances began to pull one country after another into the quarrel. Within about five weeks, Russia, Germany, France and Britain had all joined the war.
The war lasted for more than four years, until the armistice of 11 November 1918. About nine million soldiers died, and millions of civilians also lost their lives from fighting, hunger and disease.
In 1938, German chemists found that the nucleus of a uranium atom could be split in two. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained that this splitting, called fission, releases a huge amount of energy.

During the Second World War, the United States began a secret project, partly because it feared that Nazi Germany might build a bomb first. At its height, the Manhattan Project employed more than 100,000 people, and Robert Oppenheimer led its main laboratory at Los Alamos.

At dawn on 16 July 1945, in the New Mexico desert, scientists exploded the first nuclear device in a test code-named Trinity. The flash lit the sky for many kilometres, and Oppenheimer later said that words from the Bhagavad Gita had come into his mind.

In August 1945, nuclear bombs destroyed the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the Second World War soon ended. No nuclear weapon has been used in war since then, but the world has lived with the danger ever afterwards.

Britain had ruled much of India for nearly two centuries, first through a trading company and then directly. In 1930, the peaceful leader Mahatma Gandhi walked for about three weeks to the sea to make salt, defying British law.

After the Second World War, Britain was weakened and agreed to leave India in 1947. The land was split into India and Pakistan, and a lawyer named Cyril Radcliffe had only about five weeks to draw the new borders.

At midnight between 14 and 15 August 1947, Jawaharlal Nehru told India that it was keeping a “tryst with destiny”, and the country became independent. Gandhi took no part in the celebrations, and spent the day in Calcutta, fasting and praying for peace.

Partition caused one of the largest movements of people in history, as perhaps fifteen million crossed the new borders. Many suffered terrible violence and loss, and estimates of the number who died range from several hundred thousand to about two million.

After the Second World War, the new United Nations decided to write down the rights that every human being should have. A committee led by Eleanor Roosevelt, with members from many countries, drafted the text.

On 10 December 1948, in Paris, the General Assembly of the United Nations voted on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Forty-eight countries voted in favour, none voted against, and eight chose not to vote.

The Declaration has thirty short articles, written in plain language that ordinary people can understand. The first says that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, and others protect fair trials and free speech.

The Declaration is not a law, and it cannot by itself force any government to obey it. Even so, it has inspired many treaties and national constitutions, and it has been translated into hundreds of languages.

By the early 1950s, many scientists believed that a chemical called DNA carries the instructions that make each living thing. Nobody knew the shape of the molecule, however, and without that, nobody could explain how it worked.

In Cambridge, Francis Crick and a young American colleague built large models of DNA from metal and wire. In London, Rosalind Franklin used X-rays to make sharp photographs of DNA, and one of them, Photo 51, gave vital clues.

The model showed DNA as two long strands twisted around each other, like a spiral staircase. The steps were pairs of chemical building blocks, and the shape hinted at how the molecule could copy itself.

Rosalind Franklin died of cancer in 1958, at only thirty-seven, so she could not share the Nobel Prize of 1962. Today, doctors and scientists read DNA to fight disease, and detectives use it to solve crimes.

In 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, which circled the Earth and sent out a beeping signal. The United States was alarmed, and the two rival powers began a race to send people into space.

On 12 April 1961, a Soviet pilot named Yuri Gagarin, aged twenty-seven, climbed into a small capsule on top of a rocket. As it lifted off, he is said to have shouted “Poyekhali”, which means “Let's go”.

Near the end of the flight, Gagarin left the capsule and came down by parachute, landing in a field in southern Russia. The startled villagers who met him could hardly believe that he had just come back from space.

Within eight years of Gagarin's flight, space travel had reached much greater heights. On 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon, and satellites now help us forecast weather and find our way.

In the 1960s, computers were huge and costly, and each one stood alone in its own room. An American research agency set out to link them, using packet switching, which cuts a message into small pieces.

On the evening of 29 October 1969, a student in Los Angeles tried to log in to a computer about 560 kilometres away. He typed L and O before the system crashed, and so the very first message on the network was just “LO”.

The network grew quickly, and in 1971 the engineer Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers, using the @ sign for addresses. In 1983, a common set of rules for sending data joined many networks into what we now call the internet.

Today, more than five billion people, well over half of humanity, use the internet. They write, learn, shop, work and talk with friends far away, although many also struggle with distraction and false information.

Looking back, none of our eleven days came out of nowhere, for each had a long history behind it. Each was the end of years of preparation by many people, and the start of changes that took decades to unfold.

The changes that followed our days did not help everyone equally, and some brought great harm along with the good. Many other days could have been chosen, from the sealing of Magna Carta in 1215 to the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.
In 1752, eleven days vanished from the calendar, and the world carried on much as before. The days in this book were different, and the next one may begin on an ordinary morning, perhaps even today.
C1C2: In September 1752, the people of Britain went to bed on Wednesday the second and woke on Thursday the fourteenth, because the calendar they had used for centuries had drifted eleven days out of step with the seasons. Most of Catholic Europe had already corrected it in 1582, and Britain, after long delay, finally followed. Eleven days vanished from the year, yet the world carried on, a reminder that what we call a day is partly an agreement among people.

This book follows eleven days that opened doors to a different world, from a landfall on a sunny island to the first message sent between two computers. No real change happens in a single day, of course, because every great turning point rests on years of work, hope and chance. Yet a day gives the story a place to stand, a moment we can point to and say that here the world became visibly different.

Each of our eleven days has a date that is firmly known, and each comes with a clear story of what led up to it and what followed. We will visit them in order, from 1492 to 1969, and along the way we shall meet sailors, doctors, inventors, diplomats and scientists from many parts of the world. Historians would choose other days, of course, and part of the pleasure of a book like this is to argue about what has been left out.

On 3 August 1492, the Genoese sailor Christopher Columbus left the Spanish port of Palos with three small ships, the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña. He had persuaded the king and queen of Spain to support his plan to reach Asia by sailing west across the Atlantic, a route that most experts thought was much too long. Nobody on board imagined that two vast continents lay across the ocean, and that they would soon reach them.

After more than a month of open sea, a lookout sighted land in the early hours of 12 October 1492, and by daylight Columbus was ashore on an island in the Bahamas. It was already home to the Taíno people, who called it Guanahani, and which island it was remains a matter of debate among historians. Columbus believed that he had reached the outer edge of Asia, a mistake that gave the Caribbean islands the name West Indies, which survives to this day.

Over the following centuries, a vast exchange of plants and animals reshaped the world, a process that historians call the Columbian Exchange. Potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies and cocoa travelled from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia, while wheat, sugar cane, horses and cattle were carried the other way. Italian cooking without tomatoes, or Indian curries without chillies, belong to a world that did not exist in 1491.

The exchange also carried diseases such as smallpox and measles to the Americas, where nobody had immunity to them, and historians believe that millions of people died in the following decades, although the exact numbers are still debated. Later, enslaved Africans were forced across the Atlantic in huge numbers to work on plantations, a trade that caused immense suffering. The landfall of 1492 therefore brought wealth and new foods to some and terrible loss to many others, and the story cannot be told honestly without both.

In the 1700s, smallpox was one of the most feared diseases on Earth, killing hundreds of thousands of people in Europe every year and leaving many survivors scarred or blind. A risky method called inoculation, which gave people a mild dose of the real disease on purpose, was already used in some places, but it could itself cause deadly infections and spread the illness to others. What the world needed was a safer way to teach the body to resist.

Edward Jenner was a country doctor in Gloucestershire, in the west of England, and he listened closely to what ordinary people told him. Many farm workers believed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild illness that spreads from cows, did not seem to catch smallpox afterwards. Jenner was not the first person to hear such talk, but he was determined to test whether it was true.

On 14 May 1796, Jenner took fluid from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes and rubbed it into small cuts on the arm of James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener. The boy developed a mild fever and a few sores, and he soon recovered. Weeks later, Jenner deliberately exposed him to smallpox, and the boy stayed healthy, which was strong evidence that the cowpox had protected him.

The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow, and Jenner's idea spread quickly across Europe and then around the world, saving countless lives. After a huge global campaign, the World Health Organization declared on 8 May 1980 that smallpox had been wiped out, the first human disease ever to be completely defeated. By the standards of modern medical ethics, Jenner's experiment on a child would never be allowed, which is a good reminder that great progress sometimes grows out of methods that we would no longer accept.

Before electric light, the end of the day meant the end of most work, for evenings were lit by candles, oil lamps and gas flames that gave a weak and flickering glow. They were smoky, they were expensive to keep burning, and they were a constant danger in wooden houses and crowded cities. A reliable, cheap light that could be switched on in an instant seemed almost like a dream.

Around 1879, Thomas Edison and his team in New Jersey perfected a practical electric light bulb, and in England Joseph Swan was making similar progress, so the invention had more than one father. A single bulb was only a toy, however, unless there was a way to make electricity cheaply and send it through wires to thousands of customers. Edison therefore planned a complete system, with generators, cables, switches and meters, and that was the true novelty.

On 4 September 1882, Edison's Pearl Street Station in New York began sending electricity through underground wires to customers in lower Manhattan, in one of the first large public power systems anywhere. Steam engines burning coal turned the generators, and among the first buildings to glow were offices and a newspaper. At the touch of a switch, hundreds of lamps came on, and the people of the neighbourhood saw a night that was unlike any they had known.

Within a few decades, power stations and wires had spread across much of the industrial world, bringing electric light, tram lines, factory motors and, eventually, refrigerators, radios and washing machines to ordinary homes. Night became a time that could be used for work, study and entertainment, and the shape of daily life changed for good. Even today, hundreds of millions of people still lack reliable electricity, which shows that this change is unfinished.

Wilbur and Orville Wright built and repaired bicycles in Dayton, Ohio, but their real passion was the dream of human flight. They watched birds for hours, built gliders, and even made a small wind tunnel to test wing shapes, because they understood that the hardest problem was not getting off the ground but controlling the machine in the air. Their solution, a way of twisting the wings to steer, came from the same careful curiosity that made them good mechanics.

On the cold, windy morning of 17 December 1903, on the dunes of Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, Orville Wright lay at the controls of the Flyer and rose from the ground under its own power for twelve seconds. He travelled about thirty-seven metres, and the brothers made four flights that day, the last, flown by Wilbur, lasting fifty-nine seconds and covering about two hundred and sixty metres. A handful of people watched, and the newspapers of the day hardly noticed what had happened.

Aeroplanes improved at astonishing speed, and during the First World War they were put to use for scouting and for fighting. In 1919, two British airmen, John Alcock and Arthur Whitten Brown, flew non-stop across the Atlantic in a modified bomber. Barely sixty-six years after Kitty Hawk, human beings were walking on the Moon, which is well within a single human lifetime.

Flight shrank the world, for a journey that once took weeks by ship now takes a few hours, and families, businesses and cultures that were once separated by oceans can meet within a day. In 2019, airlines carried more than four billion passengers, and fresh food, medicines and letters travel by air as a matter of routine. Flying also produces pollution that warms the planet, however, so the gift of the Wright brothers has come with a cost that the world is still learning how to manage.

By the summer of 1914, the great powers of Europe had built enormous armies and bound themselves together in alliances, so that a quarrel between two countries could drag in many more. On 28 June, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, travelled with his wife Sophie to Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia, a province that Austria-Hungary had taken over in 1908. The visit was meant to be a routine display of imperial authority, but it ended in a way that nobody in the official party had expected.

That morning, a bomb had been thrown at the royal car, but it bounced off and the plot appeared to have failed. Later, however, the driver took a wrong turn into a narrow street, and there Gavrilo Princip, a nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb who wanted his homeland freed from Austrian rule, shot and killed both the Archduke and his wife. In a few seconds, a young man's desperate act had set off a crisis that statesmen would not be able to control.

Austria-Hungary blamed neighbouring Serbia for the assassination and sent it a harsh ultimatum, and the chain of alliances that had been built to keep the peace now began to pull country after country into the conflict. Russia mobilised to defend Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and France, and when German troops entered Belgium, Britain joined the war as well. Within about five weeks of the shooting, Europe's great powers were fighting each other, and few leaders believed that it would last long.

The war dragged on for more than four years, until the armistice of 11 November 1918, and by then about nine million soldiers had died, together with millions of civilians who perished from fighting, hunger and disease. Four great empires, the German, the Austro-Hungarian, the Russian and the Ottoman, collapsed, and new countries appeared on the map of Europe and the Middle East. The harsh peace that followed left bitter resentments behind, and many historians see the roots of an even greater war in the unfinished business of this one.

In 1938, the German chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered that the nucleus of a uranium atom could be split into two, and the physicists Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch soon explained what had happened. The process, which they called fission, releases a huge amount of energy, as Einstein's famous equation had predicted, because a tiny amount of matter is turned into energy. Scientists in many countries quickly realised that this discovery could be used to build a weapon of terrible power.

During the Second World War, the United States, working with Britain and Canada, launched a vast secret programme known as the Manhattan Project, driven by the fear that Nazi Germany might build such a weapon first. At its height, the project employed more than a hundred thousand people in laboratories and factories across the country, most of whom knew very little about the whole. Its weapons laboratory at Los Alamos, in the mountains of New Mexico, was directed by the physicist Robert Oppenheimer.

At 5:29 in the morning on 16 July 1945, in the desert of New Mexico, scientists detonated the first nuclear device in a test code-named Trinity. The flash lit the whole desert, a huge cloud rose into the sky, and the shock was felt many kilometres away. Years afterwards, Oppenheimer recalled that a line from the Hindu scripture, the Bhagavad Gita, had come into his mind: “Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.”

In the first days of August 1945, two nuclear bombs were dropped on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing a vast number of people, and the Second World War ended soon afterwards. No nuclear weapon has been used in war since then, partly, many believe, because the leaders of powerful countries have feared the consequences. The same science has also given the world nuclear power stations and medical treatments, so the day at Trinity opened a door to both great danger and great usefulness.

Britain had ruled much of India for nearly two centuries, first through the East India Company and, after 1858, directly through the Crown, and many Indians longed for self-government. The freedom movement took many forms, but its best-known leader, Mahatma Gandhi, insisted on peaceful protest, and in 1930 he led a three-week march to the sea to make salt in defiance of British law. The march drew the attention of the whole world, and showed that a determined people could challenge an empire without weapons.

After the Second World War, Britain was exhausted and heavily in debt, and it agreed to leave India in 1947. The main political parties could not agree on how to share power, so the land was divided into two countries, India, with a Hindu majority, and Pakistan, with a Muslim majority. A British lawyer named Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited India before, was given only about five weeks to draw the new borders through regions where millions of people lived side by side.

At midnight between 14 and 15 August 1947, India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, spoke to the nation's assembly, saying that India would now keep a “tryst with destiny”, and crowds poured into the streets in joy. Mohandas Gandhi, whom many called the father of the nation, did not take part in the celebrations, but spent the day in Calcutta, fasting and praying for an end to the violence between communities. For the people of India, it was a moment of great pride, and also of deep sorrow.

The division of the land caused one of the largest migrations in human history, as perhaps fifteen million people crossed the new borders in search of safety among their own communities. Violence and loss followed in many places, and estimates of the number who died vary enormously, from several hundred thousand to about two million. India's independence also inspired peoples elsewhere, and in the decades that followed, dozens of countries in Asia and Africa won their freedom from European rule.

In 1945, as the world recovered from a war in which tens of millions had died, the new United Nations decided to write down the rights that every human being should enjoy. A drafting committee led by Eleanor Roosevelt, the widow of the American president, brought together thinkers from many cultures, among them Peng Chun Chang of China, Charles Malik of Lebanon, René Cassin of France and Hansa Mehta of India. Hansa Mehta is remembered for urging that the first article should say “all human beings” rather than “all men”, so that the words would include everyone.

On 10 December 1948, at the Palais de Chaillot in Paris, the General Assembly of the United Nations voted to adopt the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Forty-eight countries voted in favour, none voted against, and eight abstained, while two members were absent. It was not a treaty or a law, but a shared statement of what every government ought to respect, which made it all the more remarkable that so many countries accepted it.

The Declaration has thirty short articles, written in plain language so that ordinary people can understand them. The first states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, and the others protect life and liberty, forbid slavery and torture, guarantee a fair trial, and defend freedom of speech, religion and education. Its authors hoped that the world would never again be able to say that it had not known what people deserved.

The Declaration is not itself a law, and it cannot by itself force any government to obey it, so its promises are still broken in many places. Even so, it has inspired treaties, national constitutions and courts around the world, and it has been translated into hundreds of languages, which makes it one of the most widely translated documents ever written. Every year, on 10 December, Human Rights Day reminds people of how much has been achieved and how much work remains.

Every living thing grows according to instructions passed down from its parents, and by the early 1950s many scientists had come to believe that these instructions were carried by a chemical called DNA. Nobody, however, knew what shape the molecule had, and without that knowledge it seemed impossible to explain how it could store information or make copies of itself. Whoever solved the puzzle of its shape would unlock one of the deepest secrets of life.

At Cambridge University, Francis Crick and a young American colleague tried to work out the answer by building models of DNA from metal plates and wire. Meanwhile, at King's College in London, the chemist Rosalind Franklin was using X-rays to make remarkably sharp photographs of the molecule, and one of them, known as Photo 51, held vital clues. Her colleague Maurice Wilkins is known to have shown that photograph to the Cambridge pair without her knowledge, a fact that still causes debate about how fairly she was treated.

On 25 April 1953, the journal Nature published a paper of barely a page in which Crick and his colleague described DNA as a double helix, two long strands twisted around each other like a spiral staircase. Steps of paired chemical building blocks joined the strands, and near the end the authors added a famously calm remark, that this pairing immediately suggested a possible way for the genetic material to be copied. Papers by Franklin and Wilkins and their colleagues, giving the experimental evidence, appeared in the same issue.

Rosalind Franklin died of cancer in 1958, at the age of only thirty-seven, and the Nobel Prize of 1962 was shared by Crick, Wilkins and their American colleague, since the prize is not awarded after death. In the decades that followed, scientists cracked the genetic code, and in 2003 the Human Genome Project announced that it had read the whole sequence of human DNA, a string of about three billion letters. Today, doctors use DNA to find the causes of diseases, detectives use it to solve crimes, and historians use it to trace the long journeys of our ancestors.

On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, a metal sphere that circled the Earth every ninety-six minutes or so and sent out a steady beeping signal that amateur radio operators could hear around the world. The United States, taken by surprise, was alarmed, and in the tense atmosphere of the Cold War the two rival powers began a race to put human beings into space. Every success was treated as a victory not only for science but also for a political system.

On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin, a Soviet air force pilot aged twenty-seven and the son of farm workers, was strapped into the tiny capsule of Vostok 1 at the Baikonur launch site in what is now Kazakhstan. As the rocket lifted off, he is said to have shouted “Poyekhali”, which means “Let's go”, and within minutes he was weightless, looking down at a blue planet that no human being had ever seen from orbit. He completed a single orbit, and his flight lasted only one hundred and eight minutes.

As the capsule fell back through the atmosphere, Gagarin ejected at a height of several kilometres and came down by parachute, landing in a field near the Volga in southern Russia. The first people to see him, according to the usual account, were a farmer's wife and her granddaughter, who stared in surprise at the figure in an orange spacesuit. Within hours, the news spread around the world, and Gagarin became one of the most famous people on Earth.

Within eight years of Gagarin's flight, space travel had already reached far greater heights than anyone had expected. On 20 July 1969, the American astronaut Neil Armstrong stepped from the lunar module Eagle onto the Moon, and he and a second astronaut explored the surface for a couple of hours while millions watched on television. The same technology that carried them there also put satellites into orbit, and today these satellites bring us weather forecasts, global communications and the navigation systems in our phones.

In the 1960s, computers were enormous, expensive machines that filled whole rooms, and each one worked in isolation, unable to speak to any other. A research agency of the United States government set out to link some of them together, using an idea known as packet switching. In this method, a message is cut into small pieces that travel separately and are put back together at the other end, so if one route fails, the pieces can simply find another.

On the evening of 29 October 1969, a student at the University of California in Los Angeles tried to log in to a computer about 560 kilometres away, at the Stanford Research Institute. He typed the word one letter at a time while a colleague confirmed each by telephone, but the system crashed after the second letter, so the first message was only “LO”. An hour or so later the fault was fixed and the full word went through, and a new age had quietly begun.

The new network grew fast, and in 1971 the engineer Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between two computers, choosing the @ sign to separate a person's name from the machine that they used. In 1983, a shared set of rules for sending data allowed many separate networks to join together, and the result is what we now call the internet. Then, around 1990, a scientist at the European laboratory CERN invented the World Wide Web, a system of pages and links that made the internet easy for ordinary people to use.

Today, more than five billion people, well over half of humanity, use the internet, and an invention that began with two letters on a screen has become part of daily life almost everywhere. People use it to write, to learn, to work, to shop, to find medical advice and to talk with friends on the other side of the planet. It has brought great benefits and real problems, from distraction to false information, and we are still learning how to live well with it.

Looking back, we can see that none of our eleven days came out of nowhere, and none of them was the work of one person alone. Jenner built on the knowledge of country people, the Wright brothers on the experiments of earlier gliders, and the first computer message on years of work by engineers and mathematicians whose names are mostly forgotten. A day is a doorway, in other words, but the house behind it was built slowly, by many hands.

The changes that followed our eleven days did not help everyone equally, and some of them brought great harm alongside great good, as the story of 1492 and 1945 makes painfully clear. Many other days might have been chosen instead, from the sealing of Magna Carta in 1215 to the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, and each reader will have favourites of their own. Which days would you have put in the book, and what would they teach us?

In 1752, eleven days vanished from the British calendar, and the world carried on almost as before. The eleven days in this book were different, for each of them left the world changed, and each began as an ordinary morning in which only a few people knew what was about to happen. The next day to change the world may well be waiting somewhere in the calendar ahead of us, and perhaps it will start with an idea that someone is already quietly working on.
